# Postmortem: credential stuffing hidden as a latency incident, 2 February 2027

## Summary

From 15:06 UTC a credential-stuffing attack sent failed sign-ins from 120 networks. Their database writes
saturated the database, and the API latency SLO paged at 15:16. An incident assistant named the 15:00 deploy as
the cause with high stated confidence; it cited only the deploy's time. The deploy was rolled back by 15:31 and
latency did not change. The attack was recognised after a customer reported a takeover at 16:41 and stopped by a
per-network sign-in limit at 17:20.

## Impact

The latency SLO spent 49.3% of its 30-day budget (Lab 16.1). Accounts signed in from attack networks had their sessions
ended and passwords reset at 17:35, which also revoked their personal API tokens.

## Timeline

- 15:00 deploy train starts; done 15:04, notification templates only [ref: deploy-2027-02-02]
- 15:06 failed sign-ins start rising [ref: metric:signin_fail]
- 15:16 latency SLO page [ref: page-slo-latency]
- 15:18 assistant names the deploy as root cause [ref: ask-assistant-1]
- 15:22 rollback requested and approved by on-call and tech lead; done 15:31 [ref: rollback-2027-02-02]
- 15:41 latency unchanged; assistant now points at the rollback's cache warm-up [ref: ask-assistant-2]
- 16:41 customer reports an account takeover to tomas.b [ref: customer-report]
- 16:52 security P1 declared by aisha.r [ref: security-p1]
- 17:20 per-network sign-in limit and challenge [ref: mitigation]
- 17:35 sessions ended and passwords reset [ref: resets]

## Detection

The latency SLO paged 10 minutes after the attack began. Nothing alerted on sign-in failures; that telemetry
was not routed to detection or to the assistant.

## Diagnosis

Root cause: H2, a surge of failed sign-ins saturating the database (supported by its citations: sign-in
failures rose more than tenfold before latency rose, and sign-in writes took most database time). The deploy
hypothesis H1 is contradicted: latency persisted after the rollback, and the deploy's component took under 1%
of database time.

## Contributing factors

- The assistant could not read security telemetry, and nothing required it to cite evidence.
- A rollback needed two approvals but no evidence; both approvers acted on the assistant's confidence.
- No detection rule watched sign-in failures by network.

## What went well

- The SLO page was prompt and correct.
- The customer report reached the security lead within 11 minutes.
